questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Types of Farming' refers to.
questions.a: Farming in India is broadly classified into primitive subsistence farming, intensive subsistence farming, and commercial farming based on the purpose, scale, and level of technology used.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Types of Farming'.
questions.a: Subsistence farming is practised to meet the needs of the farmer's family; commercial farming uses modern inputs and grows crops for the market.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Types of Farming' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Introduction

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Cropping Patterns' refers to.
questions.a: Cropping pattern refers to the proportion of area under different crops at a point of time. Major patterns include rabi, kharif, and zaid crops grown across different seasons.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Cropping Patterns'.
questions.a: Rabi crops are sown in winter and harvested in spring; kharif crops are sown with the monsoon and harvested in autumn; zaid crops are grown in the short summer season.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Cropping Patterns' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Cropping Pattern

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Major Crop: Rice' refers to.
questions.a: Rice is the staple food crop of a majority of the people of India. It requires high temperature (above 25 degrees C), high humidity, and annual rainfall above 100 cm.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Major Crop: Rice'.
questions.a: Rice is a kharif crop grown in the plains of north and north-eastern India, coastal areas, and deltaic regions; it is also grown in areas of less rainfall with irrigation.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Major Crop: Rice' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Major Crops

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Major Crop: Wheat' refers to.
questions.a: Wheat is the second most important cereal crop and the main food crop in north and north-western India. It requires a cool growing season and bright sunshine at the time of ripening.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Major Crop: Wheat'.
questions.a: Wheat is a rabi crop needing 10-15 degrees C at sowing, 21-26 degrees C at harvest, and about 75 cm annual rainfall; major producers are Uttar Pradesh, Punjab, and Haryana.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Major Crop: Wheat' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Major Crops

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Millets and Pulses' refers to.
questions.a: Millets (jowar, bajra, ragi) are coarse grains grown in dry regions with low rainfall. Pulses (tur, arhar, gram, urad) are leguminous crops that enrich soil fertility by fixing nitrogen.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Millets and Pulses'.
questions.a: Millets are hardy crops suited to arid conditions; pulses are the major source of protein in the Indian diet and restore soil nitrogen.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Millets and Pulses' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Major Crops

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Food Crops vs Cash Crops' refers to.
questions.a: Food crops (rice, wheat, millets, pulses) are grown to provide food grains; cash crops (cotton, jute, sugarcane, oilseeds, tea, coffee) are grown primarily for sale and industrial use.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Food Crops vs Cash Crops'.
questions.a: Food crops meet dietary needs while cash crops generate income and supply raw material to industries.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Food Crops vs Cash Crops' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Major Crops

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Agricultural Development and Green Revolution' refers to.
questions.a: Agricultural development means increasing farm output through modern inputs and technology. The Green Revolution introduced High Yielding Variety (HYV) seeds, chemical fertilisers, and irrigation to boost food grain production.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Agricultural Development and Green Revolution'.
questions.a: The Green Revolution of the 1960s sharply increased wheat and rice production in India through HYV seeds and modern inputs, mainly in Punjab, Haryana, and western Uttar Pradesh.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Agricultural Development and Green Revolution' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Agricultural Development

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Impact of Globalisation on Agriculture' refers to.
questions.a: Globalisation has opened Indian agriculture to world markets, bringing new technology and export opportunities but also exposing farmers to competition from subsidised imports.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Impact of Globalisation on Agriculture'.
questions.a: Globalisation offers better prices and modern inputs for some crops, but small farmers face challenges due to reduced subsidies and competition with cheap imports.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Impact of Globalisation on Agriculture' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Impact of Globalisation on Agriculture

concepts.title: Contribution of Agriculture to the Economy

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Contribution of Agriculture to the Economy' refers to.
questions.a: Agriculture is the backbone of the Indian economy, providing livelihood to about two-thirds of the population, supplying raw materials to industries, and contributing to exports.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Contribution of Agriculture to the Economy'.
questions.a: Agriculture supports food security, employment, industrial raw material, and export earnings; its share in GDP has declined but it remains the largest employer.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Contribution of Agriculture to the Economy' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Contribution to National Economy

questions.q: Explain in your own words what 'Sustainable Agriculture' refers to.
questions.a: Sustainable agriculture is farming that meets current food needs without compromising the ability of future generations to meet theirs, using practices that conserve soil, water, and biodiversity.

questions.q: State the single key point to remember about 'Sustainable Agriculture'.
questions.a: Organic farming, crop rotation, mixed farming, and reduced chemical use protect natural resources and ensure long-term productivity.

questions.q: Under which section is 'Sustainable Agriculture' taught, and from which source text?
questions.a: Sustainable Agriculture
